utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good morning to you. Appearances -- Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

This morning we have with us our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? I see none.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We have discussed this, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser and myself, and we feel it is our responsibility for this case and also for the future to state that -- put on record, rather, our unhappiness at the way the Prosecution conducted or finalised its filing of the final briefs. It's regrettable. It caused us a lot of inconvenience, and we just hope that this will never happen again. But let's not waste more or lose more time on this. Yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just state for the record that the Prosecution also regrets the inconvenience caused to the Trial Chamber and also caused to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I'm sure you do, Ms. Sellers. I had never any doubts in my mind. Just also so that the public will be aware why we are starting late this morning, there was a technical fault with the video recording system. I thank the technical staff for having found a remedy to that earlier than expected. So, of course, the time that you have lost, Ms. Sellers, you will be able to recover on Friday, and if that is not possible, then on Monday. We have allowed still -- kept Monday in -- open for any further submissions that may become necessary. Yes. Who is going to address the Chamber? Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be addressing the Chamber first, and I'll be followed by co-counsel Gramsci di Fazio and during, of course, possibly of later today or tomorrow, Ms. Joanne Richardson will be addressing the Trial Chamber. If I might, I would like to start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Today the Trial Chamber will hear the closing arguments of both parties in the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber will address the crimes committed against Bosnian Serb victims in Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and early 1993. The Trial Chamber will take the serious duty of adjudicating the evidence that has been adduced against Naser Oric as a perpetrator of those crimes. Your Honours, we would briefly like to recapitulate the Prosecution's case in this introduction to you. Before doing that, we would like to state that the role of the International Criminal Tribunal for Yugoslavia has the obligation to prosecute irrespective of the perpetrating party, irrespective of whether the aggressor eventually becomes the victor or the victim of the armed conflict. It is that solemn duty that you have been charged with in this case. In the mid-1992 period, in Srebrenica municipality, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and until 1993, there was the outbreak of armed conflict. The armed conflict was both civil and international. During the armed conflict in that region, Serb villages were attacked, civilian houses were burned and destroyed, civilian property such as barns, such as livestock, was also attacked and destroyed. And Serb civilians and Serbs who might have been participating in this armed conflict were taken as prisoners to the town of Srebrenica. It is during those battles in 1992 and 1993, but even prior to the battles that are in the attacks that are in our indictment that Naser Oric was considered a hero, a valiant defender, a brave resister. Now, Your Honours know that there is no doubt that these attacks took place. The Prosecution alleged that within the attacks of Rakovica, Jezestica, Fakovici, Bjelovac, Kravica and the surrounding hamlets that crimes took place. And there is not any reasonable doubt that these villages were destroyed, that they were burned, that the inhabitants could not come back and live in those villages after the attacks. The Prosecution has shown that the attacks were organised, they were planned, they were carried out from one location, with soldiers moving from Srebrenica to attack the village. They went across at times confrontation lines, went into the land of the other fighting party, the territory. Groups, various groups, joined together, attacked in unison. Now, we would like to remind the Trial Chamber in several different manners that these were not attacks led by civilians rising en masse. This is not a levee en masse to defend themselves from invading forces. That's the reason that we are using the word specifically. They were attacking forces. These were not incidents of spontaneous uprisings, they are incidents of planned, organised attacks. No one was approaching their village. These soldiers went to other villages. The very opposite of levee en masse. The fighters, and at times they are misnomered. They are called Muslim fighters, they are called members of the Territorial Defence, members of the army of Srebrenica, members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These soldiers in the attacks that the Prosecutor has alleged were under the control, the effective control of Naser Oric. During the attacks they inflicted wanton destruction. Destruction that is beyond military necessity, beyond what was legal. Therein, crimes were committed. They also detained prisoners, mistreated them, in some cases murdering them after they were brought back from Srebrenica -- brought back into the town of Srebrenica. The Prosecution's case against Naser Oric as a commander is because he is responsible for the crimes committed by his subordinates and at times he aided and abetted the commission of the crimes. Burning and destruction was a pattern and became a policy. Serb prisoners were a necessity in order to exchange, exchange for Muslim soldiers, exchange for Muslim dead soldiers at times. The real question that is before Your Honours, real questions of this case, is whether Naser Oric was the commander of these forces, did he have effective control, and if so, did he fail to prevent or punish these crimes? That's what Your Honours are going to be looking at. That is the evidence that has to be evaluated and put into the proper legal framework. The answer to each of those questions is yes. The Prosecution's evidence proved that Naser Oric was the commander of the subordinates who committed the crime. And the Prosecution's evidence proved that Naser Oric exercised effective control over those subordinates. The Prosecution's evidence has also proved that Naser Oric failed. He failed to prevent crimes of wanton destruction in the Serb villages, and he failed to prevent murders and cruel treatment that took place in the detention cells in Srebrenica. Naser Oric failed to prevent, he failed to punish, those who committed the crimes. The Prosecution's evidence has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Naser Oric is guilty as charged for those crimes against Bosnian Serb victims, as alleged in the Prosecutor's amended indictment. Now, the Prosecution will not take the opportunity during these closing arguments to recount every fact. The Trial Chamber has seen numerous oral pleadings, heard many witnesses, you have received 92 bis statements, you received 94 bis statements, you have seen expert witnesses, you have called your own expert. You have also had the benefit of final pleadings, written and now oral. You have been paying careful attention to the facts. The Prosecution has noted the questions that you have asked and at times the corrections that you have made in the questions that we have asked. We know that you have been attentive. What we will try and do with this closing argument is to clear the smoke in the burning villages that the Defence would prefer that you surround yourself in. We will attempt to untie the double knots of contradiction that permeates the Defence theories. We hope to give you those valuable turning points as one looks at the evidence, as one ponders the evidence, to understand that it only leads in one direction, and that will be a conviction for Naser Oric. Naser Oric was a commander of the Srebrenica armed forces. The documents do not camouflage that truth. They reveal that truth. Hence the importance of accusing them to be forgeries, to be false, to be kept out at any price. Naser Oric had effective control over his subordinates. The Prosecution claims and has proven that he chose not to exercise it. He chose not to prevent or punish. Naser Oric knew of the crimes against Serbs and he chose to ignore them. He should have known. He should have known of the crimes, if he didn't actually know. The truth is he knew and he chose at times not to avail himself of the information because he didn't want to incur the wrath of his soldiers who were very loyal to him. And he did not want to incur the wrath or possibly further heartache of Muslim civilians who had lost much during the war. He chose not to respect the law at the cost of the Serbian victims. Naser Oric had the reasonable means, the material ability, he had the use of communication, multi-levels of communication, both within the Srebrenica enclave and, when necessary, to reach outside of the enclave. He had the use of institutions that didn't function perfectly but that functioned sufficiently in order for him to prevent or punish or in the very least make inquiry to discipline those who were insubordinate. He chose when to use but most important he chose when not to use, when to ignore this material ability. He used it for other things but not to punish crimes committed against Serbs. Now, before the Prosecution proceeds to the few selected facts that it would like to put forward to you in its closing arguments, I would like to make three stops at legal street lights. The Defence showed these lights, positioned these lights, in the wrong direction. They did not shine where they could clarify what Your Honours need to understand. They played with the shadows. The first of the legal stop lights is the levee en masse. What is a levee en masse? In many ways it's a very nice descriptive term that even we as lawyers and often as lay people describe an event, spontaneous uprising, people are defending themselves, or consistent defending, that's a levee en masse. We can use it loosely outside of the Trial Chamber. We can use it loosely in the street. It's a wonderful sound bite for journalists. Your Honours have to use it within its legal meaning. A levee en masse is a concept under international humanitarian law because it relates to whether certain persons will get protection, the protection of humanitarian law. And while it's quite recognised that members of regular armies become prisoners of war, there is a question in humanitarian law whether persons who spontaneously take arms to defend their villages, should they be afforded those same protections as soldiers? Hence the invention of the concept of levee en masse under humanitarian law. I would ask Your Honours to join with me in carefully analysing what is a levee en masse. The legal meaning. The levee en masse relates to inhabitants of non-occupied territories who, on the approach of the enemy, spontaneously take up arms to resist the invading forces without having had time to form themselves into regular armed units. It's a short-term solution. Now, the Prosecution concedes that there it was a levee en masse in Srebrenica. It happened around April 17th, probably up until May 17th, various groups, that when Serbs were coming into their town, into Srebrenica, took up arms to expulse them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm speaking of 1992. Thank you for the clarification. That short-term levee en masse is what gives us our self-organised groups and even gives us some of the heroic profiles of some of the persons in those groups. A levee en masse does not have a command structure due to its spontaneous nature. A levee en masse is preorganisation. The then-fighters in Srebrenica decided to become soldiers, more organised combatants, and hence the levee en masse in Srebrenica ends in the Prosecution's point of view certainly, for certain groups, on the 20th of May. Now, the Srebrenica fighters, after the 20th of May, decided to do two things that levee en masse certainly does not countenance. They decided to name a commander, decided to set up a staff, decided to give themselves a name, Territorial Defence. 25 days later they decided to incorporate more people, more groups, within their organisation and start to set up detachment services, military police, military war hospital, communication system. That's not a levee en masse, Your Honours. The Defence would have us believe that the levee en masse continued throughout 1992, throughout 1993. It's impossible. It didn't happen. Your Honour, I would also like to point out to you that the levee en masse concept depends that the enemy is approaching. The attacks that we have charged on the armed forces of Srebrenica, the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica, approaching other villages. There is no factual basis for a levee en masse. Even if some witnesses have come with the very best intentions of describing fighters, combatants, rag-tag bearers of arms in March of 1993 or April of 1993 as levee en masse, that was a descriptive term absent of its legal significance. Inapplicable to the situation we have. Ambassador Arria with the best intentions responded that yes, there was a levee en masse. And he extended it, not just to Srebrenica but when one looks at the testimony, and that's transcript page 14330. He testified that the BiH army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was more like a levee en masse than an army. That's incorrect, although well intended. And even the testimony of Mr. Tucker was mistaken in his characterisation of a levee en masse being present in Srebrenica in March of 1993. Well intentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I stop you here, Ms. Sellers, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree also that you did not re-examine either one or the other after their testimony to contest this to them, both Pyers Tucker and Ambassador Arria?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, we agree to that. And also the reason we agree to that, those were descriptive terms. We were not challenging them on the legal significance of the term at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the street light that shows levee en masse as being a reason, a justification, or proof of why there was no command structure in Srebrenica will misguide you, will lead you down the wrong street. It is legally inapplicable and even its descriptive terms do not assist us in our endeavour. I would now like to move to the next street light where we need clarification, and that is the difference between necessity and military necessity. Your Honours are well aware of the 98 bis decision, and certainly in that decision, you made a pronouncement. And if you would permit me to read it. "The Trial Chamber found on page 4 that it did not require further evidence from the Defence regarding" -- and this is in quotes: "The urgent necessity for the Bosnian Muslims to attack villages and hamlets named in the indictment in order to try and secure food, medicine and weapons for the purpose of the survival of the Muslim population in Srebrenica. This limitation does not in any way mean that the Trial Chamber does not require any further evidence that the Defence may wish to advance in relation to the aspect of military necessity to engage in wanton destruction as alleged in Counts 3 and 5 of the indictment." There is a distinction that you've made between military necessity and what you are referring to as necessity in the attacks. Now, the question of necessity in the attacks, necessity to attack, jus ad bellem not jus in bello, can one attack, not what does one do during the attack, cannot be conflated as the Defence has tried to do. The Defence confuses the necessity resorting to force, let's say even going into the attacks, even though we are in an armed conflict within Bosnia-Herzegovina and the concept of military necessity. In its closing brief, it cites that there was a vital military necessity to launch the attack, to save the civilian lives from Serb attacks and to avert death from starvation, shelling. A more imperative justification for an action cannot be imagined. Bjelovac was without question a military objective. This is not the same thing as military necessity in terms of wanton destruction. As a matter of fact, they have enlarged the ideal of what Your Honours was referring to as necessity more in a general sense in trying to make it a military necessity to attack in a broader sense. Can I stop for a moment? Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I just was looking around because I heard a noise coming from somewhere and I don't quite know what it is. And I'm saying it because at a certain point in time, also, the transcript that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appears on the main monitor -- I just saw a part of it being highlighted and that's something that we cannot do ourselves on that monitor, so two curious things happened. So anyway, let's proceed. I don't want to interrupt you in any way, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the Defence goes on to state in relationship to the attack of Bjelovac that the Prosecution never mentioned a single word to the Trial Chamber about the horrific suffering of the Muslim population in the area. For those Muslim civilians, in December 1992, Bjelovac meant death by starvation or shelling. There was no alternative for them but to attack. The Prosecution maintains that if it did not mention the horrific suffering, it was for the reason that this justification for the Srebrenica armed forces to resort to armed force in Bjelovac in the first place was not legally relevant. Your Honours did not say, Show me the military necessity of the attack. It's not relevant to the question of whether Naser Oric's forces conducted themselves in a legal manner during the attack in accordance with humanitarian law. This distinction that Your Honours have set out in the 98 bis is a distinction that goes in many ways to the heart of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and humanitarian law. Whether you be a levee en masse, whether you be a regularly formed army, it is how you conduct yourself in war that we examine in terms of war crimes. The Defence would have the justification for attack, which is not part of our Statute. We do not have the crime of aggression, although the war in this instance has already started. The Defence would have you look at that to be the justification for anything that occurred during the attack. But we know, Your Honours are well aware, I preach to the choir here, that you cannot deliberately attack civilian objects. We have appellate jurisprudence on that, Hadzihasanovic. But it's a very well known doctrine of humanitarian law. To conflate the entire town of Bjelovac as a legitimate military target is to allow for attacks to occur on civilian objects. To say that the entire town of Fakovici, Rakovici must be attacked and whatever happens there is military necessity is to allow in the back door attacking of civilian objects. Your Honours in your 98 bis set forth a standard that's being misinterpreted. For those reasons, the Prosecution has chosen just to remind you and to shine light in a different direction, to allow us to get back to the central issue. What was legitimacy of the conduct of Naser Oric's subordinates during the attacks? They committed crimes, Your Honour. They committed wanton destruction that was beyond the military necessity of the acts during the attack and right after. If I might also now walk you to our third street light. And that's the issue of coordination. And I'm going to speak about coordination on two different opportunities. In this first opportunity, I'd like to draw your attention to the Defence's use of coordination, what they have cited in their closing brief, is coordination in relationship to the overall control when determining the existence or not of an international armed conflict. Your Honours, and particularly I have to say, Judge Agius, because you've written the Brdjanin decision, understand that there is discussion, elements, of the role of coordination when one wants to find the overall, the overall control that another state might have over the army in a third state. That's just part of the test of international armed conflict. In order to determine that overall control, one looks at factors of coordination, coordination of that army in the third state. The Defence in raising this issue to say that coordination as cited under the Tadic decision was leading in our case is extremely misguided, if in the misleading. The Tadic Trial Chamber decision that talked about coordination was overturned by the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision. The Tadic Appeals Chamber decision said that coordination, overall coordination in relationship to international armed conflict can be a factor in establishing whether that second state governs the army and the armed forces of a third state. They were not speaking about coordination in relationship to command as Your Honours must discuss, must evaluate, under Article 7(3). Your Honour, I think I'm quite certain that the coordination of the international armed conflict, the Defence would be more than willing to concede. They have agreed with the evidence that we've led on Gow to say that the armed conflict that occurred in Srebrenica had elements, relationships, ties, to Serbia, Serbia and Montenegro. It is not this coordination that the Trial Chamber has to be concerned with. So we would just like to shine the light there for a second. I would now ask you to consider that the ability, the ability to misread the law, might affect the ability to evaluate and understand the facts on the part of the Defence. If they are mistaken, then one has to readjust. If this is their intentional reading of the law, then Your Honours will just have to find that to be erroneous. The Prosecution will proceed now with its body of arguments. I'd just like to outline those for you. First, the evidence of Naser Oric as a commander will be reviewed together with the evidence of a selection, small selection, of his subordinates, those that I call the wild bunch, because that's how we've been led to believe that they are. We will look at coordination as it relates to command again, under Article 7(3), in its proper sense, its proper context. Next, the Prosecution will continue to address the convincing relevant documents that prove Naser Oric's guilt and that cannot be unlinked, cannot be seen without the totality of all the evidence. And subsequent to the authenticity of documents - and I say authenticity in its broadest sense, Your Honour, I'm not just speaking of forensic handwriting examination - the Prosecution will return to a few pertinent issues related to the crime base. We will not go day by day or verse by verse. We will rush you to some areas that need to be revisited. The attacks in the villages, the murders and the cruel treatment in the prison, you're well aware of how they occurred. We just like to comment on how they must be viewed in the judgement. There will be certain points about effective control that we would also like to revisit with you. We've place arguments in our closing brief and in the replies, as has the Defence. We would like to speak a bit more about communication and the reasonable means available to Naser Oric. Prior to concluding, the Prosecution will finally turn to evaluation of witness testimony. We would like to thank you in advance for your attention and, of course, we are available for your questions. We proceed by stating the Prosecution does not deny Naser Oric or the people of Srebrenica the right to defend themselves. They are denied the right to destroy wantonly. There is a right to detain persons of the enemy during an armed conflict. There is no right to mistreat them, including murder. The Prosecution's case has focused on those elements and has proven those elements beyond a reasonable doubt. Your Honours, right now I'd like to return to the issue of Naser Oric as a superior. The evidence is irrefutable. Naser Oric was a superior. In the very least, if we just go with the Defence's put forward, he's a superior of the Potocari group. He's a commander there. The Potocari group is a bit more extensive than the 15 or 20 lads that hung around him. But, Your Honours, that's not the truth. Naser Oric was a commander, a superior, of a much larger force, an increasingly growing force; ever since the 20th of May, 1992, the Srebrenica Territorial Defence, and then the Srebrenica armed forces. Now we have laid that out in both the closing brief and elements of the reply. The Srebrenica Territorial Defence, one could look at as being de facto. It wasn't anointed from Sarajevo or Tuzla when it was first created. It's not de jure, it's not legitimate. It's only an election. Naser Oric assumed responsibility, commandership after being elected. And others became subordinate to him. I'd like to remind you of the testimony of Becir Bogilovic, one of the few witnesses that we have who was present at the meeting. Judge Agius questioned him and said, you asked: "When the members present at that meeting had an option of two persons to choose from as commander, what did they really have to choose about? A person who would then do what? Be what? And don't try avoid answering my question. The delegates there had two persons to choose from, Naser Oric and the other one, Ustic." Mr. Bogilovic says: "Yes." Judge Agius then says: "And they chose Naser Oric. They chose him as what? Mr. Bogilovic responds: "To be commander." Judge Agius then asks: "Commander of what?" And Mr. Bogilovic says: "Of the staff of the Territorial Defence." Judge Agius's next question is: "Well, which would include whom?" And then Mr. Bogilovic says: "Which would include the villages that were present." The Prosecution agrees. There is a transcript at 6512 through 6513. The villages that were present on the 20th of May. Later on, other villages, other what were self-organised groups decided to join the Srebrenica Territorial Defence. Now, the Defence at times would have us believe that the meeting didn't take place, or if it took place, Naser Oric wasn't elected commander; or if he was elected commander, that the groups that were under him stayed those minimal groups from Bajramovici throughout the entire armed conflict. The contrary, the contrary, the absolute contrary, is true. That's the beginning, in the very least, of the de facto organisation. That's the beginning of Naser Oric being commander and in a sense larger than just the Potocari lads. Naser Oric moves on to command not only the Srebrenica TO, the army, the 8th Operational Group, he remains as a commander until the end of the armed conflict. At times he's referred to as colonel, more often as commander. Your Honour, there is no person better to talk about the truth, the Bajramovici meeting, what occurred there, how the staff was developed, tasks that the staff undertook, than Commander Naser Oric himself. I would ask you to draw your attention to this short video. Your Honour, could you wait one more minute? There is no sound. We are having slight technical difficulties also. Your Honour, I believe we are getting assistance from the booth.

utterances.text: One moment. If we could stop, rewind to where we should be starting, in other words, at 12 minutes 13.4 seconds, so that the interpreters can -- are not taken by surprise and they can start translating at the ordinary pace. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica, the cultural centre and the cultural club Srebrenica, I call the commander of the 8th Operations Group, Mr. Naser Oric, to open. Before, before I begin, I want to greet everyone present and congratulate all fighters and people on Kurban Bajram. Dear guests, officers, and soldiers, we have gathered here today to mark the day when the staff of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence was founded, the staff that developed into a command body of the Srebrenica armed forces, and the formation and the command of the 8th Operations Group of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the structure of the 2nd Corps. Such gatherings are always an opportunity to recall the very beginning of the war. Precisely 25 months ago, the people in Eastern Bosnia fell into a trap of unilateral fascist wave poisoned with nationalist ineradicable barbarianism in the centre of Europe, a story that has lasted 25 months so far and I do not know how long still, of the Muslim Bosniak people cannot be told at one such gathering, I hope this time, without demagogic approaches, but I must remind you that two years ago today the staff of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence was founded. "Leaders, the then-municipal and party politicians, the bare-handed Muslim people entered a defence war unrecorded in history. Self-organised, the first battles began on the 20th of April, 1992, in Potocari followed by the defence of Suceska on the 1st and 2nd May, 1992. The combat in the town of Srebrenica on the 5th, 6th and 7th of May, a sabotage on the 7th of May, 1992, in Potincenje near Ormace, the first combat actions at Vidikovac on the 8th of May, 1992, and on the 15th of May, 1992, in the region of [inaudible]. On the 16th of May, 1992, the combat at [inaudible] and so on. The combat success commanding officers of the self-organised units met two years ago to this day in Bajramovici and established a joint command of the entire [inaudible] of the Srebrenica staff. "I will not bother you today with all the tasks and decisions performed by the staff in the past period. I shall just mention that the staff members had to perform for us the duties that for the enemy were done by the generals of the notorious former Yugoslav People's Army together with all the support services. utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's the Presidency, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that hereby adopts this, order of assignment. There is other business to take care of before arriving at the name of Naser Oric, and what is that business? The establishment, appointments of commanders. Zenica, the Vitez municipality, Doboj. When we get to page 5 and we see Naser Oric, it should strike you, it should strike you, that unlike the other municipalities, there is only one name, only one person, who is being named to the position of the municipal Staff Commander. Unlike in the other municipalities where you at times have one, two, three, four, five, the recognition is that Naser Oric, to the establishment position as municipal Staff Commander, another de jure recognition of his superior position as commander. Your Honour, who signs this? It comes from the Presidency, signed by the president. So is Naser Oric a commander or superior? Prosecution has proved that beyond a reasonable doubt. Is Naser Oric acting as a commander, reporting to authorities, partaking in military battles? Certainly, Your Honour. Your Honour, Naser Oric later on, in the beginning of November, agrees with his further appointment as commander of the subregion. Now, the Defence has admitted to this fact. This is not a contested fact. In the Prosecution submission of the 65 ter pre-trial brief the Defence agreed, yes, there was appointment of Naser Oric as commander in November 1992. The issue might be how well did the subregion function; but the issue is not whether he was a superior, at whatever level the subregion was functioning. And the Defence, in agreeing to this fact, certainly, along with Your Honours and the Prosecution, recognise that Naser Oric didn't then shift from being the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces. That position wasn't given to anyone else. He remained commander of the Srebrenica armed forces, commander of the subregion. He is acquiring more and more superior authority. Your Honour, the fact that the Defence admitted to Naser Oric's position might lead one to think that it was very logical, it's not contested. One has to see that commanders were named to further command. Naser Oric was a commander who had loyalty, respect, control. He was successful in battle. The Srebrenica armed forces was gaining territory, not losing territory. Srebrenica was becoming a magnet, a centre. The military centre of the Srebrenica enclave. And so yes, he would be named the commander of the subregion, very logical. He had enough power that some of the men who surrounded him could assume political positions in the subregion. Now I'm not entering into the functioning of the subregion, I'm entering into the existence of Naser Oric's superior authority within that entity. As a superior, Naser Oric, in particular, with some internationals, is known as the commander. With others, he chooses not to be known, he chooses not to be present, chooses to have others go before him. And it's a choice. If you remember the film that you've seen concerning the delivery of food in November 1992, Naser Oric is present. He's present along with the War Presidency, with other members of the political elite in Srebrenica, but he's present. If you remember, when the different members from CanBat came, some of the witnesses really hadn't met Naser Oric, imagined that their superiors might have been dealing with him. He was there. He could have made himself available at times. Obviously Lieutenant-Colonel Rex Dudley requested Sead, on three or four occasions, could we please -- could I please meet him? So he had to make his evaluation in the absence of Naser Oric. Was Naser Oric too busy? Yes, he was at the front lines, doing what? Leading, commanding forces, organising. Or he was at the staff headquarters, or in Potocari. No matter where he was physically, he was not out of his position as a commander. Well, how do we know that? Because at times he did choose to meet the internationals who came during that time period. And if one would remember the testimony of Mr. Tucker. Your Honour, I'm at page 5802 of the transcript. This is the examination of Pyers Tucker. The question is: So President Izetbegovic made it clear that the details of getting into Srebrenica enclave was something that they could facilitate? He was not emotional or histrionic. He gave every impression of being a professional soldier in a very difficult situation. He was in strong command of his men. I'm now on page 5833 of the transcript. Question: Did you -- of the men accompanying Colonel Oric, did any of them introduce themselves to you? Answer: No. None of them introduced themselves. It was very clear from their behaviour and body language and the way they talked amongst themselves that they were subordinates and that Colonel Oric was the man in charge. utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honour, at this Tribunal, Article 7(3) let's us know that it doesn't suffice just to be a superior. If you're a superior and you have no subordinates, this Tribunal's jurisdiction has Article 7(1), under which your liability can be established. Under Article 7(3) the question is whether you have subordinates, the effective control you have over your subordinates, so that if they commit crimes, or if they are about to commit crimes, and that you knew or should have known, and only when you failed to prevent or after the commission of crimes you failed to punish, the liability can attach. Now, it's true that Naser Oric is being held for both 7(3) and 7(1) responsibility. The 7(3) responsibility incurs for the attacks that occurred, Rakovici, Jezestica and the crimes that occurred in the prison. This 7(1) liability is alleged when he is present at the attacks. Right now I'm going to direct your attention to subordinates, a crucial condition for 7(3) liability. And although the discussion of subordinates in particular goes toward having sustained the element that the Prosecution was required to prove, I'd like Your Honours to look at it a bit broader, that Naser Oric had subordinates that he was able to influence and effectively control. Now, many of the documents of the Prosecution has submitted before Your Honours shows lists of subordinates, everything from the Stari Grad unit, the Osmace unit, the Potocari unit. There we see hundreds of persons who the Prosecution alleges and has proven were subordinates to Naser Oric. Why? Because they came under the Territorial Defence. They came and were subsumed and subordinated to him under the Srebrenica armed forces. When Naser Oric's command staff becomes part of the larger ABiH army, he doesn't lose his subordinates. They now fall into the hierarchy, the military chain of command, of the ABiH. Enver Hogic is certain about this. There are no loose subordinates running around if they are under the control or under the authority of a commander of the ABiH, and Naser Oric was such a commander as of August. But I would like to draw your attention to a small subsection of the subordinates, and I have called them, not for lack of better name but for the reason in the manner in which they seem to be portrayed here, as the wild bunch, and those are the local commanders that were so independent, so unable to be controlled, that witness after witness was asked, could they take orders? Do they act on their own? Could Naser Oric conceivably be superior? Who am I speaking about? I'm speaking about Akif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Ahmo Tihic, Ejub Golic, Mirzet Halilovic and Kemo from Pale, Kemo Mehmedovic. My comments will be brief because I'm sure Your Honours will remember the numerous witnesses who came to attest to their independence. The Prosecution sets forth the following proposition that the evidence has proved. Yes, they all had strong personalities. These were men who had a sense of independence. It's for that reason that they became local commanders, that they were considered local commanders. Nevertheless, each one of these fiercely independent personalities subordinated themselves to whom? To Naser Oric. Some were more willing than others. Some were rather reticent but they did it. Zulfo Tursunovic, ever since the Bajramovici meeting, subordinated himself to Naser Oric. As a matter of fact, it was Zulfo who then spoke to Hakija Meholjic who was not at the meeting and convinced him, Come on, Hakija, join us, Oric is the commander, Akif Ustic is going to be his deputy, come on, be a part of us. They probably thought that there would be some of their command that they would have to relegate to Naser Oric and a bit of their independence, and you felt that natural tension between them. But they subordinated themselves, not only to Naser Oric but to Akif Ustic, Naser Oric's deputy. Ahmo Tihic, one of the early members of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence Staff subordinates himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
