utterances.text: The situation of Ejub Golic and the men from Glogova is different. They were not at the Bajramovici meeting, but they soon joined Naser Oric as subordinates. Why? Because the organising force of Naser Oric and his subordinates was among their highest hopes on how to recapture Glogova, and that was a good bet. Being in Cizmici, having contact, going to Jezestica, eventually the priority came to take Glogova back. Now, much has been made about, did Naser Oric appoint Ejub Golic a commander? No, couldn't have been. Well, both could happen. They are not incompatible. He was a de facto commander, in quotes, elected by his men. His men might not have countenanced any other local commander. That doesn't mean that Naser Oric as an ABiH commander couldn't send out an order and make that a de jure position. Now, Your Honours, I think that you must have the impression that there was very little paper in Srebrenica. There might have been less paper but there wasn't a complete dearth of paper. But it didn't mean that an order was replicated 50 times, passed to each soldier. Oral conveyance, oral communication, of orders or decisions occurred much more frequently and could be considered just as valid. The Prosecution maintains that Ejub Golic subordinated himself to Naser Oric and became the de jure commander over the Glogova unit, and he had been that de facto. Now, the subordination of these very independent men led to insubordination at times. Army forces expect perfect subordination and are ready for insubordination, and that's what discipline is about. If it didn't occur, there wouldn't be instances of disciplining insubordination in rules and regulations in armies throughout the world. In particular, in Srebrenica, there might not have been the complete absence of insubordination, even among the local leaders, but that did not mean that they were not subordinated to Naser Oric. Akif Ustic is killed in October. There is testimonies that say, Why did he go off? Why did he do this independent act that led to the death not only of Akif Ustic but some of his men? That insubordination was not praised, it was lamented, that insubordination was viewed as something that could be life threatening and dangerous. It was not heralded. When Naser Oric decided to exercise control, he exercised control over these men also. Hakija Meholjic testified of being surrounded the hotel Domavija was surrounded by Naser Oric's men, armed. They later on resolved their differences. Ejub Golic was eventually arrested. This was way after demilitarisation. Naser Oric assisted in letting him be free because he needed him as a fighter. Your Honour, there was a relationship between very strong-willed local commanders, who could, who could, demand the subordination of their men when they went into battle. Did people shift in between units sometimes? Yes. Did an order have to come out about that? Yes. But Naser Oric tactically used a very good tool. The vice-presidents were people everyone admired and would follow into battle. Naser dealt with the vice-presidents. The best way to subordinate the troops was to give them a leader that they admired, the in between. Now these men who were too independent, too wild, what did they do? They showed up to meetings, they took their men to the attacks. When they decided not to go into an attack, such as Hakija did at times, they would give men. Their men would be subordinated to the commander at the attack. Subordinated to Naser Oric. Hakija Meholjic is quoted in our brief. I believe it's on page 2.000 -- sorry, 6853 in March. Naser Oric subordinates him and then subordinates other local commanders under him to hold the front line. These strong characters helped keep the Srebrenica army cohesive. And that's why we have the folklorism, Ah, Hakija's men, Akif's men. That assisted, that didn't destroy the command and control. But my primary purpose is so that you understand that these men were subordinates, chose to be subordinates, did not take their men and go off. Their men became part of the Srebrenica armed forces. And that's because Naser Oric, as a commander, had strength, was able to attract them, was able to maintain them. When questions arose, and you see it in P8 4, Naser wanted to resign, No, no, no, Naser, you're my commander, you will always be my commander. But what they wanted Naser to do a bit more was choose to use his effective control. Coup d'etats against Naser Oric, he speaks about them. In all, the very independent man kept the independent men subordinate to him. I would now like to turn to Mirzet Halilovic as a subordinate of Naser Oric. Another independent man, can't control him. It's amazing the uncontrollables that flocked to Naser Oric. Mirzet Halilovic, he and Naser obviously were good acquaintances before. I don't know if they were karate buddies, but they were good enough acquaintances that Naser brings back from Belgrade a uniform for Mirzet Halilovic before the war starts. Now, Mirzet Halilovic is named a commander of the military police. And let there be no doubt, this occurred before the setting up of the Srebrenica War Presidency. We see the document on June 15th, and then later on the decision is recounted in other documents dating from the beginning of July. Mirzet Halilovic was part, not of the 15 or 20 lads from Potocari but probably the dozens and dozens of lads, fighters, soldiers, Potocari, Budak, Pale, that come under the Potocari TO. And Naser Oric states in his suspect interview that Mirzet was beginning to be a bit of a problem because they had people coming in from Glogova. They had other refugees coming in, joining these Territorial Defences, and Mirzet wasn't necessarily acting in a correct military manner. In the suspect interview, P329, Naser Oric says: "Once I was called by the War Presidency that there was chaos broken out in the town and that the main problem in the town was the military police, that they didn't do anything, and that what which they are supposed to do and they are doing some dishonourable things, among others, that Mirzet Halilovic had begun to act like his own commander, that he wasn't obeying any orders either from Ramiz or from Hamed Salihovic, simply that he was behaving like a sheriff, just on his own, and there was suspicion." He goes on to talk about suspicion that the prisoner who had died had not simply died, that he had on one evening, he had been in a drunken state, he got drunk, and that he had gone into the prison cell and beaten this prisoner, and after this, he had had, and after beating, he had succumbed to his injuries. Your Honour, I bring this up not to discuss the prison scenario. I bring this up to the very important phrase that Naser Oric says that he wasn't obeying any orders either from Ramiz or from Hamed Salihovic. Those are men who are on the armed forces staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can you be specific, Ms. Sellers, as to the reference part of -- from 329?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On my Word transcript, 3 page 2. I will have to get you the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we need. If not for us, at least for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, so within that phrase, within that group of sentences, Ramiz Becirovic and Hamed Salihovic are members of the armed forces staff, direct subordinates of Naser Oric and Mirzet Halilovic. They can issue orders to him, and now the complaint is that he's not obeying orders. And the War Presidency is conveying this information to Naser Oric. Just as the War Presidency conveyed information in August when they were discussing Mirzet Halilovic and how he was acting in the town of Potocari. Now, it's very crucial that we understand that according to the Defence theory Mirzet Halilovic is subordinated to the War Presidency. Do we ever see a witness that says: Hajrudin Avdic has issued various orders Mirzet Halilovic in August? Ms. Djilovic certainly didn't type any up. There is an order from the War Presidency within what we refer to as the military police log, P458 or P561, but what's astounding is the dearth of orders, communication between the War Presidency and Mirzet Halilovic. And when he is finally placed under Mr. Bogilovic, it is Mirzet Halilovic the person and not the military police staff. If there is some confusion that it's a military police staff, that confusion is rectified in that interfollowing period between October 15 and November 22nd. The military police belonged to the military. But Mirzet Halilovic is one of the wild bunch. But Naser Oric had chosen him to be the chief of military police, knowing that he had problems in Pale. Naser Oric is not afraid nor too challenged to be around very independent military men. It's part of how the structure is constructed. The frustration belongs to his subordinates who are on the armed forces staff. Their frustration at the local commanders and with Naser Oric comes up, led almost to resignations. That the commanders aren't using their effective command, not that they are aren't commanders and not that the commanders aren't subordinate to Naser Oric. The OS staff doesn't deal with any of these commanders individually as supreme leaders. For good reason. They are not. Your Honour, on several occasions, the question has been raised: Who was the military police subordinate to? There is one person who knows better than the others, and that's Mr. Bogilovic. Even Hakija Meholjic, by the time he takes over the police during demilitarisation, is talking about the civilian police, because he becomes head of a demilitarised police, saying that there were no files, there was nothing. The military police had files. You have those files before you. The military police had persons stationed in units. You have some of those documents before you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Judge Agius asked Mr. Bogilovic: "Who did you say that you found out in November that was subordinated to the army and not the presidency?" And Mr. Bogilovic answered: "The police staff. It was subordinated." Judge Agius then says: "The civilian police or the military police?" The answer is: "The military police. The civilian police remained under the War Presidency or, rather, the president personally throughout." Then I ask: "Could the military police then make the decision, make decisions independent of any civilian authorities, to your knowledge?" I'm directing my question to Mr. Bogilovic. And he says: "The military police could make some decisions but only within the framework of their military authority." I'm at transcript 63 -- 6332 to 6333. Your Honour, even if we go to the other scenario, and let's just say, for argument's sake, that the military police served both functions, the Srebrenica armed forces and the War Presidency, maybe there were sometimes when they were mixed, we know that when Atif Krdzic is appointed that that mixture is over. We know that if the mixture occurred, it occurred after October 14th when the crimes in the first period of detention, September to October, are basically over and before the crimes in the second detention centre began. We also know that even if they are mixed, that does not preclude that Mirzet Halilovic remained subordinated to Naser Oric and that he has responsibilities to prevent, to punish, to exercise effective control. The Prosecution's position is that the military police was under Naser Oric, he appointed the commander, he chose at times not to utilise effective control, and that the relationship of the military police to the War Presidency might be one of information sharing because it was another police force in the town that had to interact at times with the civilian police force. Because Becir Bogilovic, who becomes head of security for a second, would you take that trouble-maker away? Becir didn't order any of the other military policemen to do whatsoever in their functions. Is there confusion in P84? Yes, Your Honours, there is. The confusion is resolved quite quickly. Mirzet Halilovic is probably one of the more colourful characters, in one sense, personality-wise, in Srebrenica and the one who commits crimes. He's the one who wears a cowboy hat; remember? He's replaced by Atif Krdzic, a man who was a subordinate prior to being named chief of the military police and who remains a subordinate of Naser Oric's throughout his period as a superior. Your Honour, there was a question of mistranslation that the Defence rose in terms of the interview of Naser Oric, and that was whether the translation was correct about the military police or Hamed Salihovic being charged with interrogations, and I'm talking about transcript page 14664. The Prosecution's position is that even if that translation is corrected according to what the Defence says, that just means that the military police and Naser Oric are under the same military command. That does not change subordination. Your Honours, in terms of Kemo from Pale, Kemo Mehmedovic is sent by Nedeljko Radic, and Kemo Mehmedovic, as his correct name, we have fully briefed why we believe that he is a subordinate of Naser Oric, a subordinate because he comes from the Territorial Defence of Potocari under Pale, under Budak, and also because he becomes a member of the Specialised Intervention Platoon in November/December. Kemo is probably someone who has a violent nature. People always comment about how he and his brother were extremely dangerous, violent men, nationalists, before the war. The evidence shows that during the war, he kept to character. This was well known. Kemo from Pale, is, was, at that time period, a subordinate of Naser Oric, another one of the wild men. Your Honours, I would briefly like to address you later on about effective control over the men. This segment just concentrated on the identification of those subordinates. But prior to leaving this section and turning it over to co-counsel, Gramsci di Fazio, I want to return back to coordination. Coordination now as a part of command under Article 7(3). Your Honour, do we have to check and see if the alarm is meaningful to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I can assure you that this is the Monday, noon alarm in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless I am informed otherwise but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, as now I have stated several times, Naser Oric was a commander, and one of the tools he use was coordination, and coordination was a normal -- as a matter of fact, a recognised doctrine in order to execute military operations. And the Prosecution's position is that command necessitates coordination. From the moment you have more than one unit, I think I would go as far as to say from the moment you have more than one subordinate, you might be doing coordination on some level. Coordination does not denigrate, doesn't diminish, and it certainly is not a substitute for command. I would propose to Your Honours to look at P84.1 as a book that in many ways deals with coordination. Coordinating not only the different units, in terms of tasks for ambushes, to reconnoitre, to be present at this attack, coordination for who will be going to Tuzla. Coordinations for which kitchens get food and which percentage. Your Honour, coordination is part of command, as used in the Srebrenica armed forces. Now, to the extent that Naser Oric had independent-minded local commanders, coordination became the most effective tool. Better to say let's coordinate, let's see if we can work out a way where we can all do this together. That goes down much better with independent-minded people, particularly those who are armed. It was an effective exercise of control. It didn't make the superior-subordinate relationship or a hierarchy vanish. It probably aided in the building of loyalty among the units and for Naser Oric. Now, the Defence might prefer that the Trial Chamber misread or misinterpret indications of command and coordination. Since I've already discussed coordination in the sense of overall control, when one is looking for the definition of international armed conflict, I trust that Your Honours understand that that's inapplicable in this situation. Coordination for command as discussed under 7(3) by the Defence is also inappropriate and inapplicable to our jurisprudence. The Defence brings up the case of Celebici where the commander Delalic was found to be a coordinator and therefore not in a position of command. A very cursory reading of Celebici on that point confirms that Delalic was, if I might so phrase, nothing but a coordinator. He wasn't in the army. He wasn't in a position of military command. He was coordinating between the army and civilian authorities. So while it is true that in this instance coordination did not equal command, those facts are not relevant to our facts, are not analogous to our facts. Naser Oric was a military commander who used coordination among his military subordinates. Did he coordinate with the War Presidency? He probably did that also. There is probably always a political, military discussion that had to go on in Srebrenica. That also didn't diminish his command. The Defence also cites Halilovic, and that's when Halilovic was a coordinator as chief of the inspection team. Factually inapplicable to our situation. Both cases differ. Your Honour, what is more important is looking at the JNA manuals. They promote the doctrine of coordination within command, and the JNA manuals are a military guide that all of Naser Oric's local commanders had some fleeting, fleeting acquaintance with. Will I say they were professional soldiers? No. I will say that they did their military service that year in the JNA. Were they ever coordinated among other subordinates that year? I would say the chances are 99 per cent, yes. Those who had not completed their military service, very few, were reserve police officers. They probably coordinated among their ranks also, yet stayed in a line of subordination to their superiors. Your Honour, in terms of coordination, actually removing command from Naser Oric, the opposite is true. It built command. It made him a more effective commander. It was in line with what any TO force would know, having come from the former Yugoslavia. If I just might read one part of the former JNA manual on regulations of coordination it states, and I'm reading from the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, corps of group forces, Rule 1990. We've cited that in our brief, where it says: "The commander of the corps bears the responsibility for the accomplishment of a mission. He takes decisions, gives assignments to his subordinates, organises coordination and cooperation and controls the implementation of decisions." That's on paragraph 65. Another quote says that the activities of all participants in the execution of a combat assignment are harmonised through concerted action, coordination and cooperation; thus providing for planned execution of set tasks. That's P84, Your Honour. That's what we have. Coordinated actions under command. At this time period, I would like to turn over our closing argument to my colleague, Gramsci di Fazio. Prior to doing that, I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that while we have tried to avoid a repetition of every fact, we've tried to enlighten what we believe are the important points, we are still available if you have any questions for us on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I just get the lectern, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be a break at 1.00. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, just on the question of the remainder of the day, I've had a chance to speak to my colleagues, I will go with this topic, I expect, for the remainder of today. If I luckily should finish prior to today's session, my colleagues and I are all agreed that we could stop there and finish tomorrow. We are comfortable that we will be able to do that. That's how I see today panning out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if I may suggest something, but I will not try to involve the Trial Chamber in it unless you decide to take the initiative together and in full collaboration with the Defence, the next break, as I said, will be at 1.00. I would take it that that would be a 30-minute break, which basically means that we would then reconvene at half past 1.00 only to finish at quarter to 2.00. Now, we lost half an hour this morning. If you can, in the meantime, someone will try to organise this, obtain the agreement of interpreters, technicians and all the rest of the staff, instead of having a break at 1.00, which would be a 30-minute break, we'll have a break earlier, which will be a shorter one, say, 20 minutes, but that again, I mean everyone must agree to that. If there is just one person who doesn't agree, then we will revert to -- and then we'll finish at quarter to 2.00 just the same but we would have recovered at least 15 minutes from the 30 minutes. We will still finish at quarter to 2.00, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Others need the courtroom. But perhaps the member of your staff can start coordinating with interpreters, technicians, and Defence, and if there is agreement, please let me know, and then I'll tell you when we will be stopping for a shorter break. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour. Speaking for myself, it's -- I'm happy with whatever arrangement is agreeable to all. If Your Honours please, the points that my colleague, Ms. Sellers, has made to you this morning concerning the emergence of command in the Srebrenica enclave and the position of Mr. Oric within that command structure finds its best expression in the documentation that's been produced to you in this case. In the Prosecution exhibits, you can trace the emergence of that command structure, and you can see the role that Mr. Oric played in that emerging command structure in 1992 and early 1993. Furthermore, not only can you paint the picture of the emerging command structure and his position with it, but you can actually see from time to time how he exercised his power through that existing command structure, and you can do so through all sorts of documents from the most significant documents in this case, for example, P84, to the most uneventful documents, documents signed by Naser Oric and requiring all sorts of banal day-to-day matters, the transfer of weapons, the transfer of a man, passes and so on and so forth. So the documentation in this case paints a pretty devastating picture for the Defence. It was incumbent on the Defence to try and address that, of course, and they have done so. I want to try to draw your attention to some of the arguments that they have put forward to you to show that they are really without foundation, and that the body of documentary evidence in this case remains as strong as ever and is -- remains as unanswered as ever by the Defence. The -- there have been lots of submissions and arguments concerning the documentation on all sorts of topics, but broadly speaking, the Defence seem to have launched two main attacks on the Prosecution documentary evidence in this case. Firstly, is the idea of the absence of a -- evidence of a chain of custody; and secondly, is the allegation that no witnesses have been called to comment on the Prosecution exhibits in this case. They are the two main prongs of their attack. I'm not suggesting for a moment that there are not other arguments and matters that the Defence have put forward, but in a nutshell they are the two strong planks upon which they base their argument. And furthermore, if I can put it this way, there is another, a third subcategory, and that is this: Where there is comment on some of the documents, say the Defence, that comment simply undermines the Prosecution exhibit, and I'll deal with that a little later in submissions concerning how you should approach witness testimony in this case, because it's tied up with that particular topic. So today I really want to speak about two matters: Chain of custody, and the lack or absence of commentary on exhibits. The first observation is this: The Defence have not really spelled out to you precisely how you should deal with documentation where there is no chain of custody evidence. It's not been done either in the Defence reply or in their filing on authenticity. There is certainly a lot of complaint about this topic, but there is no, as far as I can ascertain, no specific conclusion that they invite you to draw, no specific approach that they invite you to adopt. The closest they come, really, is in paragraph 15 in their filing on authenticity, where the Defence says: "There is, in fact, an almost complete lack of a proper chain of custody evidence in this case. This is one of the bases for the Defence's objections to a large number of Prosecution exhibits." Now, we are all clear that there are objections. Of course, there is no doubt about that, and strong objections on the part of the Defence, but it's not clear to the Prosecution if the Defence are saying to you, you the Trial Chamber, you must not or cannot evaluate documentary evidence where there is no chain of custody and also no witnesses commented upon the document, or whether they are saying to you that you can evaluate such evidence but that where a document doesn't have any chain of custody or what they say is a satisfactory chain of custody or no witnesses commented upon it, then you should attach no weight to it. If it's the latter, I suppose the Defence and the Prosecution are slightly closer, but if it's the former the Prosecution submits to you that they are wrong. In fact, I should clarify that the Prosecution submits to you that if they are wrong on both counts, firstly that when they suggest that you cannot -- if they suggest that you cannot evaluate such documentary evidence, and secondly that you should attach no weight at all, if that's the other argument that they adopt. And I say that for two reasons. As a matter of law, the Defence are wrong in submitting to you, if that be it, that you cannot evaluate; and secondly, as a -- when you look at the evidence in the case, and you look at the connection between the documents in this case, they are factually wrong and that there is weight that you can attach to the documents and that you should attach to the documents. If Your Honours please, this institution, and other institutions like it, will almost always have to deal with documentation that has been obtained in ways and manners and by means that are not the norm in domestic jurisdictions. In these sorts of Prosecutions, you don't have teams of forensic photographers descending upon Rakovici to take photographs on the 21st or 27th of June. They don't have police officers who are going along and speaking to witnesses and taking statements from them concerning the documentation that might have been produced on the day before. They don't have police officers who can go along and look at P84 and ask the author to come along and comment on the entries that were made at that particular time. Often documents are collected in war zones that simply make it an impossibility for that exercise to ever have been carried out. The -- in this particular case, you can see how perfectly illustrated that point is. The soldiers who went into Srebrenica in 1995 and probably collected most of the documents that are the basis of the Prosecution case, were not interested in recording where they found the document, what they were doing at the time they seized the document, the time and day that the document was seized. They weren't interested in seizing the document with a view to later using it in evidence in some proceedings somewhere. The seizures were almost always for all sorts of other purposes, military intelligence, propaganda and so on. So from the time the document comes into the hands of the power that eventually places it into a collection or an archive, all of that's lost automatically, and that feature is going to apply in many cases at similar tribunals and this Tribunal will find itself dealing with. So the reality is, for tribunals such as this, most of the archival and documentary evidence -- sorry, most of the documentary evidence that you have and is produced to you, is going to come from collections or archives, and what preceded -- the events that preceded the document going into that collection or archive or possession of an individual is often, in fact almost always, going to be lost to history. So because of that, the approach that these tribunals must take to documentary evidence is not the same as that which is adopted in domestic jurisdictions. Archival collections and private collections and individuals are often the first point of contact that investigators are going to have with material, and that's going to be years later. So right from the very start, the factual scenarios behind the obtaining of documents are such that there will almost never be a chain of custody for this sort of document. Now, of course, there are many where investigators can get some sort of evidence. I'm not suggesting it's an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. impossibility, and I'm not suggesting that these tribunals should not strive to obtain chain of custody evidence or not strive to obtain commentary on documents whenever they can. It's important that that be done. But the problem is that in the case of many classes of documents, it's going to be simply impossible right from the start. And you can see that, as I've said, in this particular case. The investigator Racine Manas testified in this case, as did the Defence witness, Madam Becirevic, I think her name was, and both provided spreadsheets, doing the best that they could, namely to show where a -- which archival collection a document emanated from. If Your Honours please, the law, I think, supports the Prosecution on this particular topic. I have given to you a copy of May and Wierda International Criminal Evidence, International and Comparative Criminal Law Series, a segment from that book. I believe that Your Honours have that. The -- I've had photocopied the section that deals with documentary evidence. And, Your Honours, it's, with respect, a very useful short overview of how to approach documentation in these sorts of cases. At 779 the authors say: "Similarly the admissibility of documentary evidence in the modern tribunals is generally governed by the same rules that govern all other types of evidence as set out in Rule 89(C)."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? MR. DI FAZIO: "That is, evidence of relevance and probative value." That, in the Prosecution's submission, is the real threshold test that you need to adopt for the purposes of admissibility in this particular case. And at 785, Your Honours can see the manner in which the sort of spreadsheet, the sort of documentation, that was offered in this case, both by the Prosecution and by the Defence, has been used in other cases. At 785, dealing with the World War II military trials in -- following the Second World War, there was a reference to the international military tribunal, and the allied documentation division, where a famous affidavit, the Kugan affidavit was prepared and used, and this affidavit was entered into evidence at the beginning of the Nuremberg trial. In addition, certificates concerning discovery and location of documents were filed along with documents to provide additional proof of authentication. The same as happened in this case. In that particular case, it would be almost impossible for the prosecutors to have adduced evidence from every person who signed every document that was used, to trace the life of the document as it passed from hand to hand, institution to institution, and eventually into their possession. But they were able to provide some documentation from that point onwards, from when it came into the possession of the prosecutors, and the same has been done here in this particular case. And it is, with respect, the best that can be done in circumstances that trials that you are now dealing with and that institutions often have to deal with can do in all of the circumstances. So that's the issue that I wanted to raise concerning the point at which there is evidence about chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I suggest that you stop whenever it's convenient, but round about quarter to 1.00 for 15 or 20 minutes, then we continue, and we finish at quarter to 2.00. And I thank everyone for having cooperated in this and make us recover about 15 minutes. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. That's helpful to me, thank you. The Defence, in their reply, suggest or seem to suggest that the Prosecution is switching positions, and I'm talking about paragraph 109 of the Defence reply. And they are talking about the evidence of Radojicic, you recall the Serb military man who came here to testify, and seemed to be suggesting that, as I understand what they say, at paragraph -- as I understand what they say at paragraph 109 of their reply, that, well, there was a chain of custody and yet when Radojicic came here it fell flat on its face and they've now switched, the Prosecution has now switched position, failed to establish a chain of custody, now switched position and saying you don't need it. Well, that's not true. When Radojicic came here to testify, if Your Honours please, he was never in a position to give you any information about what happened to the document before it fell into Serb hands. He was never in a position to do that. He couldn't have done that. And so there is in reality no switch on the part of the Prosecution case. Its position has been consistent. The Defence also provided to you, in -- referred you to Exhibit D286. I don't need you to look at it. It's a document from the Drina Corps, and it -- I think written in 1992, and it issues instructions for the proper keeping of archival materials, and I gather that what the Defence was trying to say is, Ah-hah, you see, there were mechanisms set up for a chain of custody, but there has been no evidence about it. The problem is that that doesn't solve the problem. The problem always remains the collection of -- the problem always remains that period of time between the seizure and its final resting place in the archive or the collection or the hands of the private individual who is spoken to you by OTP investigators, and so D286 does not detract at all from the Prosecution's submissions. It only shows to you what should happen after a document has been captured. So they're the submissions that I want to make to you on the issue of chain of custody evidence. The Prosecution is not submitting to you that an absence of a chain of custody is a matter that you should ignore or that you cannot take into account. It is obviously something that you can take into account and should take into account, but that's a matter that goes to the weight of the document. The weight of the document. And if I interpret the Defence submission to be in such circumstances the weight that you give to it is zero, it's nothing, then the Prosecution submits they are wrong. If the submission is that it's very little weight, well, then we are agreed. It's a question of how much weight. Then and we can argue about the facts later that -- obviously the Prosecution is going to submit to you for other reasons I'll develop later that there is much weight that you can attach to them, but in a nutshell, that's the Prosecution approach to this issue of chain of custody evidence. So can I turn now to the absence of commentary by Prosecution witnesses on its documentation. The Defence position here is clear. At paragraph 16 of the Defence filing on authenticity, they say this: "No probative value can attach to a document which has been shown to no witness." So there we are. It's a very clear expression. The Prosecution's submission is that they are clearly wrong on this. And furthermore, the Prosecution observes that there is no authority provided for this proposition put forward by the Defence. The basic starting point that you should adopt -- start from, I'm sorry, is Rule 89(C), which says that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. You would not have admitted any documents into evidence unless it had some relevant and probative value. If a document is stripped of any probative value whatsoever because it hasn't been commented upon, you wouldn't have admitted the document into evidence. The Prosecution's submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think we need to clarify this. You know as much as we do, Mr. Di Fazio, that the system that has been applied here since the beginning of this Tribunal, as regards the admission of documents, is the civil law approach, and not the common law approach. You know that in your country and my country and other common law jurisdictions how much this issue is debated at various stages of the trial, and bitter arguments and battles are fought on the admissibility of a document before it is actually admitted into evidence. Here we admit all documents with the caveat that we will decide on their final admissibility, probative value, and so on and so forth at the end of the trial, during the deliberation process. So saying that throughout this trial we admitted a large number, because we are talking indeed of a large number, of documents means that we necessarily decided that they had probative value at that point when they were admitted is not putting it correctly. Short of any challenge there and then as to the probative value of some documents, we did not of course engage ourselves in the exercise of establishing the probative value. That would be done, and it is being done, and we have gone a long way already on that, during the deliberative process. We have done that in regard to two documents at least, P65 and P68, and given strict instructions that they were not to be made use of unless further evidence is forthcoming from your side, which would make us revise what we decided as regards their probative value in relation to authenticity. That was never done, but still, P68 is referred to at least on two occasions in your final brief, which shouldn't have been done. But I want to make this clear. The fact that 600 - and I don't know how many others - documents tendered by the Prosecution have been admitted on -- with the caveat that I mentioned, does not mean that we have already at any time established to grant those documents or those exhibits a probative value. We were not asked to exclude any one in particular with -- except for 65 and 68, and a few others where we reserved our position. Ergo the bottom line would be that they are still there. Probative value and reliability and all the rest will be decided in the light of the totality of the evidence. And not just necessarily and only and exclusively on the face of the document itself. So that's the position. I hope I've made it clear. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both for you and for the Defence. Yes, sorry for interrupting you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: On the contrary, I'm grateful to Your Honour for that. In any event, if Your Honours please, certainly the Defence submission is that no probative value should be attached by you now, now, now, at the end of the case, no probative value should be attached to a document that hasn't been shown to a witness. That's how I understand the submission. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The submission, as I understand it, and as we have understood it, basically is the following: That if you have tendered a document in evidence and it has been admitted with the usual caveat and given an exhibit number, but you produced no witness to confirm either the authenticity or the contents of that document, then in the eyes of the Defence, that document has no probative value. There is no evidence -- you have not, in other words, fulfilled the obligation that you have as Prosecution, the burden of proof that you have, to prove the authenticity of each and every document that you bring forward. This is the submission, as I understand it, from the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is that I need to make this clear: Out of the 600 and so documents that you tendered, there is about 130, I didn't bring with me the statistics, about 130 of them that you never referred to any witness, right? You do, of course, refer to several of them in the final brief, but about 132 of them were not referred to or put to any witness. And similarly, the same situation more or less obtains in the case of Defence exhibits. Out of the 1.000 and I don't know how much, there are over 300 documents that you yourselves never put to any live witness. So that's the position. And, of course, we reserve our position on that. But we would love to hear all the submissions that you have in that regard, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'll perhaps just finish on this point and perhaps we can then have the adjournment. Your Honour just took away my last point. I -- one of the last points that I wanted to make on this issue, and perhaps I might as well make it now. It's been fairly squarely raised by Your Honour. That's this: The Defence itself put forward documentary evidence that the Defence itself asks you to consider as part of its Prosecution case -- as part of its Defence case, I'm sorry, I switched around. They are put forward their own documents. They say to you, Consider this evidence, evaluate it, consider it in assessing the Defence case. But they have the same quality, those documents. No witness has commented upon them, and/or there is no chain of custody. They emanate from Ms. Becirevic in the way that many of the Prosecution documents emanated from Ms. Manas. Do the Defence ask you now to ignore their case, to say that their documents have -- you can attach no probative weight to their documents? It would be -- it would not be right in the Prosecution's submission for you to do that. The Defence are entitled to have their documents considered and assessed in the light of all the evidence in the case and for you to make a decision eventually about how much weight you're going to attribute to those documents, as is the Prosecution. So the Defence -- the Prosecution finds itself in the curious position here of saving the Defence from its own submission. If Your Honours please, this would be a natural point in time for me to break. I'm proceeding faster than I thought. There is a slight possibility I'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Di Fazio. We will have a 20-minute break now. We'll start at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might. I would just like to correct the record, Your Honours. Earlier today the Prosecution team also had co-counsel Mr. Jose Doria with us. He is not with us now, but I wanted the record to reflect that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. If Your Honours please, I'll end up now on this issue of commentary by witnesses, whether it's a requirement or not, whether you need it or not in order to evaluate documents, whether you need it or not in order to give any weight to documents, whether you can rely on those documents. Firstly, I've -- you don't have to open your binders which I think have been provided to you. But from the book that I provided to Your Honours, International Criminal Evidence, at paragraph 79 -- 7.92, page 244, the authors say this: "Independent evidence, whether oral or documentary, may serve to corroborate, support, prove or disprove the authenticity and probative value of documentary evidence but it is not required." That's what the authors say there with their considerable authority. Furthermore, if Your Honours please, in the Blaskic appeal, the Appeals Chamber accepted many new documents in the -- by the Defence in the course of the appeal, many of which were unsigned, undated and came straight from Croatian intelligence archives, and the Appeals Chamber accepted those documents on the appeal and furthermore relied upon them in arriving at its decision. Do Your Honours wish me to take you through the aspects of the judgement that illustrate this, or is that submission -- I can do that now. It won't take me a moment, or -- thank you. If Your Honours please, there were four motions to admit additional evidence in that appeal under Rule 115. The Defence had filed apparently hundreds of documents as additional evidence in those motions but never put forward any witness to speak to the truthfulness or the authenticity of the documents that were filed and relied upon. And I can give you some examples. In its first Rule 115 motion they filed 288 new exhibits. You will see that in Annex A, paragraph 13 of the judgement. The Defence claimed that the documents came from various archival sources, Croatian Ministry of Defence, Office of the President of Croatia, HVO and ABiH archives. No witnesses were called from the Croatian authorities or the state archives in this regard, and you can see that at Annex A, paragraph 11 of the judgement. So as I said, they are attached to this Rule 115 motion and no witnesses were called. You can also see that at Annex A, paragraph 13 to the judgement. The Prosecution response was essentially the Defence response that has been put forward here. In its Prosecution written response, the Prosecution wrote: "The reports are anonymously written and that their veracity cannot be determined absent the testimony of the authors or recipients of these documents or other evidence supporting their credibility. Even if one considers some parts of the documents truthful, it is evidence that neither could be tested through cross-examination, nor the authenticity of these documents otherwise be established." That's the position of the Prosecution, and you can see that in their response, that -- the formal document is Prosecution response to Appellant's motion to admit additional evidence on appeal pursuant to Rule 115 dated 13 September 2001, public version, paragraph 123. The Prosecution therefore, as you can see, raised similar concerns that the Defence are raising here with you. On the 31st of October, 2003, the Appeals Chamber issued its decision admitting a number of the documents as additional evidence. So they were admitted. There was no order to have any witnesses come forward to testify about their veracity or their authenticity or the chain of custody for these particular documents. And the Appeals Chamber relied in its judgement upon some of these documents, which had been challenged on this basis by the Prosecution. And examples are Exhibit 1 to the first Rule 115 motion. Exhibit 1 -- yes, Exhibit 1 was in fact an unsigned -- this is illustrative, an unsigned, unsourced document, and no witness had testified about the document and it was admitted. And you can find the Appeals Chamber's reference in reliance to that document in its judgement, 29th of July, 2004, paragraph 342, footnote 76. And there are other examples. So the matter has been determined by the Appeals Chamber, such documents can be admitted into evidence and can be relied upon. So, in summary, therefore, the Prosecution's submission is that the Defence is plainly wrong in submitting to you that you can't or that you shouldn't look at or evaluate documentary evidence in the absence of commentary by a witness. If Your Honours please, they are my submissions to you on the chain of custody, how you should approach evidence where there is an absence of a chain of custody and where there is an absence of commentary Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by a witness. So if you accept that you can look at them, you can evaluate them, you can consider them, reflect upon them, how do you -- what should you do in order to carry out that exercise? In paragraph 7.88 of the book, it's clear -- I don't need to quote from it, but it's clear that the Musema Trial Chamber was -- yes, considered the form, the content, the purported use of the document, whether it's an original, whether it's a copy, whether it's signed, sealed, whether it's stamped or certified in any way, whether it's duly executed and so on. So one of the matters that you can use to decide what weight you will give to a document is the document itself, what jumps out at you from the page itself, and that's something that you are perfectly entitled to consider in attributing weight or not attributing weight to a document. And, of course, not all but many of the Prosecution documents in this case are originals and many are signed and stamped and have all of the features that you have come to see over the almost two years of this trial. So you can go to the document itself in order to get information and in order to carry out that exercise of assessment of weight. The other method, and a very good method in the Prosecution's submission, is to look at the connection between documents. The Prosecution submitted to you in its final brief, and I quote directly: "Many exhibits are mutually corroborating or fit into a matrix or pattern or other evidence." The Prosecution resubmits that phraseology. It puts it -- I can't put it any better than that. That makes the point nice and clearly. And we need to return now to the Prosecution final brief, and the Defence reply and revisit the submission, and there are a number of reasons for that. Firstly, unfortunately, in the Prosecution final brief, there are a number of errors concerning the connection between various documents that need to be rectified. The Defence also replied to that submission, and I want to look at one aspect of the Prosecution -- of the Defence reply. And thirdly, because, if you look at that, the point that I'm trying to make is illustrated quite simply. Yes. Your Honours don't have to look at the actual brief itself. I can tell you. It's paragraphs 35 through to the bottom of -- through to paragraph 40, pages 16 and 17 of the Prosecution final brief, and there the Prosecution was trying to illustrate to you the interconnectedness, the connection between documents, and we used a number of documents, P3, P84, P9, P57, which is unfortunately a mistake in paragraph 40; in fact, we are referring to P587. And a number of documents, P80, as well. P80, as well. That's an important document. And the way it's expressed in the Prosecution final brief is that there is a connection between all of those documents. That's not sustainable and I want to clarify that to you. There are connections between the documents but not as -- not as -- we have to be less ambitious than we were in those paragraphs, so I'd ask Your Honours to, if you come to -- if you go to revisit that Prosecution final brief, bear this in mind. Let's look at P84. On the 14th of October, this is at page 7 of the English translation. The 14th of October, there was a meeting of the operations staff and the civilian protection, and various -- you can follow through in the following pages, you can see the discussion concerning who is going to be in charge of what, and various units that are being -- the genesis of various units. At page 10, you can see that they create an agenda for the creation of various units in P84. You then look at P9 -- incidentally this is a meeting held on 14 October 1992. P9 is an order apparently signed by Mr. Oric and it basically reproduces all of the structures that you can see in P84. So the discussions occurring and then it's reflected in P9. I think it important, though, to point out just this: There is an exception. P9 refers to the creation of the Kragljivoda Brigade, whereas in P84, there is a reference to the Karacici Brigade. But other than that, I think I'm correct in saying that it mostly follows the two -- the documents and you can match them. So you can see that there are connections that are important in -- for you to look at in deciding what weight to give to various documents. In the interests of time, I think my point is made. I don't think I need to labour you with more examples of where you can find these connections. You can see them, Your Honours. I'll cut down my submissions. You can see, for example, connections between P80, which lists the -- some of the units and the formation history of various command structures in Srebrenica. P80, for example, in simple little ways, confirms other documents. There is a reference to the TO Osmace, A3 Company with 121 conscripts whose commander is Atif Sakib Krdzic in P80, and that's reflected in P570, same unit, A3, same numbers 121, same commander. You can see that. And the same applies with P80 and P571. Again, a quick cursory glance at those documents will show you how they marry with each other. The same number of conscripts, references to, in P80 to -- this is the Biljeg companies. The same commander, Ahmo Tihic, same numbers, 136. And in P571, you've got the same commander, two other documents consisting of A4 Company and A41 Company, 127 men, plus nine men, total 136. So you've got lots of connections and ways in which the documents connect with each other. It would be impossible, if Your Honours please, in the time that we have, for me to take you through, and it would just repetitive of me to start giving you example after example after example to prove the point, and I don't intend to. But I think the point is well made. However, when the Defence dealt with these submissions at paragraphs 36 through to 40, they took the view that there was no connection or demonstrated connection. Yes. And you can see where they deal with this submission at -- they deal with it basically, if Your Honours please, at paragraphs 111 through to -- they deal with it at length in their reply. I want to look at this aspect, P3. They say P3 is absolutely not confirmed by those exhibits underlined, with emphasis, and they are talking about -- one of the documents they are talking about is P9 because, of course, Prosecution raised that document to illustrate the connection between P3 and P9. You can see that really, really simply. P3 and P9 are the simplest examples that you can find dealing with this. P3 -- sorry, P9 is -- could we get it up on the screen? Yes, P9, thanks, if P9 could be made just a bit bigger. I've only got P3 in front of me and I can't read it. Thank you. Yes. Okay. P9 is -- it's order number, handwritten, 28/92 dated Srebrenica, 15th of October 1992. "I hereby order," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Then you go to P3 and you can see in paragraph 2: "I hereby order constant communication as per order number 28/92." And it's dated three days later, 18th of October, 1992; 15th of October, 1992. There you are. I just said I wasn't going to provide you with any more examples and I did. But the reason I did that was to show that the Defence reply, if Your Honours please, was inadequate. I mean, these are the connections that you can see, in so far as these two documents are concerned, at least. These are the connections that you can see between a lot of the documentation in this case, and it's something that you should really give a lot of weight to in the Prosecution's submission. Now, P -- just a few comments, if I may, about P84. I'm sorry, what time do Your Honours want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Quarter to 2.00. MR. DI FAZIO: Quarter to 2.00, thank you. Thanks. Some comments about P84. P84, if Your Honours please, was objected to early in the case by the Defence. The nature of their objection was not clear at that point, at least not to the Prosecution. However, as time progressed, it seems that the Defence seemed to have accepted that P84 is a genuine document, genuine in the sense that it truly reflects what was written in the past by someone and that it's talking about events that happened. I don't think I'm overstating the case. The Defence will correct me if I'm wrong, if I've gone too far. I'm sure they will. But that's how I understand the evidential scenario concerning P84 and the Defence attitude towards it. During the Rule 98 bis submissions, the Defence counsel went so far as to posit, suggest the author of P84. What does concern the Defence about P84 seems to be the content of it, and the submission is made in their reply that it's just -- you can't rely on this document because it's just subjective. It's someone's notes, you don't know what was really said, you can't rely on it, you shouldn't look to it, or you can't give it much weight in considering all the evidence in this case. Not so, in the Prosecution submission, not so. The very nature of the document is such that it needs -- it needs to be as precise as it can be at the time of its creation. It's obviously a log or diary dealing with matters of the utmost importance to the people living in Srebrenica. And furthermore, if you go through the document, you can see that every effort has been maintained -- every effort has been made to maintain it as an accurate and detailed account. In the Prosecution's submission, what jumps out at you from the pages of P84 is the fact that whoever had his pen out and was jotting away was trying to do a good job, trying to provide you-- trying to provide a good account, a good record, of these events. So the observation it's subjective, well, yes, that's true, subjective in the sense that someone wrote it, but it's the sort of document that calls out, requires its author, to be as objective as possible when writing down entries into it. And, of course, much of it deals with technical material, technical stuff that is not really going to be the subject of subjective -- is not going to be tainted -- it's not going to taint the document with subjective interpretation. So it's, in the Prosecution submission, a pretty reliable document, and it has connections with other documents. I've referred to one of them, as you can see, between P84 and P9. And there are other connections. So they are the points that the Prosecution wants to make about P84. Let's stand back now and look at the general approach to documentation on the part of the Defence in this case. They have -- in their reply, the Defence have expressed their displeasure at the Prosecution characterisation of a conspiracy theory about the documents. I don't know what -- quite how to approach that because I thought it was established and one of the clearest things in this case. But there is no question that right from the beginning of this case, the Defence were suggesting to you, and right through the case, the Defence have suggested to you, that the Prosecution documentation, its exhibits, are riddled with forged and false documents. They said in their opening: "So, Your Honours, you will have sift out the may false, forged and generally questionable documents which you have already heard about and which you will continue to see exposed as such during this trial." I don't intend to walk you through each and every allegation of falsity or each and every Defence witness upon being shown a document immediately pronounced it to be false. But it is fair, I think, to say, for the Prosecution to say to you, that there has been a suggestion made to you, at the beginning of this case and throughout this case, that there is -- there are bad people behind the creation of these documents, people who want to frame, for want of a better word, Naser Oric. I don't see how the Defence can escape from that. In the Prosecution's submission, it's a central plank of their defence. Yet there has not been one jot of evidence in this case about that, as far as the Prosecution can ascertain. It has been suggestion, it has remained suggestion, it is now suggestion. And there is also an opportunistic nature to the Defence approach to its handling of these supposedly suspect or forged documents. I've already made the point -- sorry, I withdraw that, the Prosecution has made the point in its brief concerning the use of documents from -- by the Defence, from challenged collections, the Sokolac collection and so on. This is puzzling in the light of what the Defence have said to you concerning the suspicious nature of these collections and puzzling in the light of what the Defence has said to you concerning the -- either the positive assertion that there has been forgery or that there may have been forgery of documents in this case. And the most dramatic example of that is when the Court appointed expert provided his testimony here in court. The Defence, of course, by then, had painted themselves into a corner. The -- some of the crucial documents in this case, the ones signed by Naser Oric, had been adjudged -- that's not the right expression. The opinion of the expert was that they were probably signed by -- I can't remember his precise language, but Your Honours will know what I mean, probably been signed by the accused. And then, of course, there is the evidence of the Prosecution expert, Dr. Fagel. There they had to make the suggestion to him that he had lost his subjectivity but there wasn't any reason put to the Court-appointed expert. That's the puzzling thing. There wasn't any reason why he should have lost his subjectivity when he is analysing these particular reports -- documents. The -- that's not exactly conspiracy theory. That's something else. That's a -- it's now moving from conspiracy theory to a suggestion that people are biased against the accused for always inexplicable reasons. And the same applied to the evidence concerning that video, the interview, the uncrowned king of Srebrenica. There, the Dutch Evangelical Church apparently and for reasons that I am still not entirely sure had somehow played a part in either the production of this material to the OTP or had somehow twisted it in some way so as to make it usable against Naser Oric for the Prosecution purposes. The final blow, though, to the conspiracy theory, and I say it's a conspiracy theory, though, comes from the forensic handwriting expert -- experts. If Your Honours please, I may want to come back to this topic briefly tomorrow but I think I can just about complete my submissions on this now. Three experts came here to testify: The Prosecution expert, Dr. Fagel, the Defence expert, Professor Bilic, and the Court-appointed expert, Dr. Kerzan. The Prosecution specifically invites you to compare the evidence of all three witnesses, all three expert witnesses, and to compare their demeanour, the way they presented their evidence and the content of their evidence. In the Prosecution's submission, the Prosecution expert was -- and Dr. Kerzan, were clearly superior to the Defence expert, Dr. -- Professor Bilic. They were clearly more moderate. They were clearly more cautious in providing their opinions to you. Professor Bilic, and I'd like to check this overnight, if I may, in case I need to add anything to it, but Professor Bilic was the only one of the Defence exhibits -- of the handwriting experts who was prepared to express himself in absolutes. He, Professor Bilic, was very, very clear. Some of these documents were definitely not written by Naser Oric. Compare that with the approach of Dr. Fagel or Professor Bilic who -- Professor -- Dr. Fagel or Dr. Kerzan, sorry, I'm having a bit of trouble with my names today. They took pains to make sure that you understood that you have to be cautious when approaching this topic, and they took pains not to express themselves in absolutes. Now, if Your Honours please, there is just one or two other points that I want to make about the handwriting experts. We've -- I'm happy to say that I've gone a lot faster than I thought I was going to today, and I'm just about at the end. Would it be okay with you if we broke, adjourned now? I can complete what I've got to say in a matter of five minutes tomorrow morning, and we are right on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's perfect with us. Tomorrow belongs to you. So we can adjourn now and we'll hear your final submissions tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning, we are sitting at 9.00, I think in this same courtroom. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there was a minor problem which I tried to sort out last week, and that was that although I had the impression that we would have -- we would be sitting four days in the morning and one day in the afternoon this week, the afternoon sitting being Friday, I was told that on Thursday we were sitting in the afternoon too. But anyway, now I can confirm to you that we will be sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon on Thursday. So that's particularly -- it's of concern to the Defence. All right? So we'll all meet, please God, tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you so much.
